overview.why: A container is not a security boundary by itself: it shares the host's kernel, so a flaw in one container can become a flaw in the whole machine. Hardening means removing every permission an application does not need, so that a break-in has nowhere to go. This is the unit that separates "we use Docker" from "we run Docker safely", and it is asked about in cloud security and SRE interviews.
prerequisites: Linux basics (permissions, processes) and Docker basics.
Some Kubernetes helps for the pod-level sections, and DevSecOps basics help for the big picture.
outcomes: Explain defence in depth for containers: Seccomp, capabilities, AppArmor/SELinux, and where each sits
Run a container as non-root, read-only and with every capability dropped except what it needs
Write a Kubernetes `securityContext` that enforces the same rules
Restrict traffic with a default-deny NetworkPolicy and limit access with least-privilege RBAC
Detect suspicious behaviour at run time with Falco rules
overview.placementTip: A strong answer to "how do you secure a container?" lists layers: minimal image, non-root user, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, Seccomp profile, network policy, secrets from a vault, and runtime detection. Practise saying them in order.

sections.title: Linux Kernel Isolation: Seccomp, AppArmor & Capabilities

content.value:
### Defense in Depth in Linux Workloads

Containers share the host Linux kernel. Hardening the system call boundary is the primary defense against zero-day container breakout exploits:

```text
Container Application ──> [Seccomp (Syscall Filter)] ──> [AppArmor/SELinux (Path MAC)] ──> [Capabilities Filter] ──> Host Kernel
```

#### Security Layers:
1. **Seccomp (Secure Computing)**: Restricts which of the ~450 Linux system calls a process can make. Blocking calls like `ptrace`, `sys_chroot`, and `keyctl` removes a large class of privilege-escalation exploits.
2. **Linux Capabilities**: Divides root privileges into granular sub-units (`CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `CAP_CHOWN`). Dropping all capabilities (`cap-drop: ALL`) and whitelisting only necessary ones prevents unauthorized packet sniffing or raw device access.
3. **AppArmor / SELinux**: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) enforcing granular file read/write, network socket, and execution permissions.

keyPoints: Containers share the host kernel, so the system-call boundary is the key line of defence.
Seccomp filters which system calls are allowed; capabilities split root into small powers; AppArmor/SELinux limit files and sockets.
Default-deny is the rule: drop everything, then add back only what the app proves it needs.

quiz.question: What is the primary function of Seccomp in Linux container security?
options: To filter and intercept system calls (syscalls) executed by a process before reaching the kernel
To encrypt container network traffic over the wire
To scan container images for vulnerable open-source packages
To manage Kubernetes RBAC token permissions
quiz.explanation: Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) acts as a kernel-level system call firewall, blocking or logging unauthorized syscalls like ptrace or reboot.

sections.title: Runtime Intrusion Detection with Falco & eBPF

content.value:
### eBPF-Powered Kernel Telemetry

**Falco** uses kernel instrumentation (via eBPF probes) to monitor system calls in real-time and trigger alerts when suspicious behavior occurs:

```yaml
- rule: Terminal Shell in Container
  desc: A terminal shell was spawned in a running production container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and container
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, dash)
  output: "Shell spawned in container (user=%user.name pod=%k8s.pod.name)"
  priority: WARNING
```

Unlike traditional log shippers, eBPF operates at the kernel ring buffer layer with low overhead, and it is much harder for user-space malware to hide from than log files in `/var/log`.

keyPoints: Prevention is never perfect, so watch behaviour at run time as well.
Falco watches system calls and raises an alert when a rule matches, such as a shell starting inside a production container.
Tune rules to your workloads, or the noise will make people ignore real alerts.

quiz.question: What does a Falco rule such as "Terminal Shell in Container" do?
options: It blocks all shells in the cluster at build time
It raises an alert at run time when a shell is started inside a container
It scans images for vulnerabilities
It encrypts container traffic
quiz.explanation: Falco watches system calls as they happen and alerts when behaviour matches a rule, such as an interactive shell starting inside a production container.

sections.title: Hardening a Container in Practice

content.value: The previous section explained the kernel mechanisms. This section applies them. The goal is a container that can do **exactly what the application needs and nothing more**. Start from the strictest settings and loosen one thing at a time only when something proves necessary.

content.title: A hardened docker run
content.value:
docker run -d --name web \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --pids-limit 128 --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 \
  -p 8080:80 \
  myorg/web:1.4.2

rows: A bug becoming root inside the container
An attacker writing tools or changing the app
Raw sockets, mounting, changing ownership and other root powers
Fork bombs and one container starving the host

content.title: securityContext for a Pod
content.value:
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault      # the container runtime's default system-call filter
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: myorg/web:1.4.2
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
          add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
      resources:
        limits: { memory: 256Mi, cpu: 500m }
Never use `--privileged`, never mount `/var/run/docker.sock` into an application container, and never mount the host's root filesystem. Each of these hands the container the keys to the machine.
Containers should be able to bind to a port above 1024 without any capability. Use port 8080 inside the container and map it to 80 outside, and you can drop `NET_BIND_SERVICE` too.

keyPoints: Run as non-root, with a read-only filesystem, no capabilities and a memory/process limit.
Kubernetes `securityContext` expresses the same rules declaratively.
`--privileged` and the Docker socket are almost always a mistake.

quiz.question: Why should production containers drop CAP_NET_RAW capability?
options: To prevent attackers from crafting raw TCP/IP packets to perform ARP spoofing or port scans inside the cluster network
To increase network throughput by disabling checksums
To allow containers to bind to privileged ports below 1024
To disable DNS resolution inside the pod
quiz.explanation: CAP_NET_RAW allows a process to create raw network sockets, which attackers can exploit for network spoofing, ARP poisoning, or covert channel communication.

sections.title: Limiting the Blast Radius: NetworkPolicy and RBAC

content.value: Hardening one container is not enough. If an attacker gets into one Pod, they will try to reach other Pods and the Kubernetes API. Two controls limit how far they can go: **NetworkPolicy** (who may talk to whom) and **RBAC** (who may do what in the cluster).

content.title: Default-deny for a namespace
content.value:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}          # every Pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]

content.title: Then allow only what is needed: web may reach the API on 8080
content.value:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-to-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: web }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
NetworkPolicy only works if your network plugin (CNI) supports it, for example Calico or Cilium. Without one, the objects are accepted but nothing is enforced.

content.title: A Role that can only read Pods in one namespace
content.value:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: pod-reader, namespace: shop }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: read-pods, namespace: shop }
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: monitoring
    namespace: shop
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

items: Avoid wildcards (`*`) in resources and verbs.
Turn off automatic token mounting (`automountServiceAccountToken: false`) for Pods that never call the API.

keyPoints: Default-deny NetworkPolicy first, then open only the paths that are needed.
Policies need a CNI that enforces them (Calico, Cilium).
RBAC: smallest verbs, smallest scope, no wildcards, no unused tokens.

quiz.question: What does a NetworkPolicy with `podSelector: {}` and no ingress rules do?
options: Allows all traffic to every Pod
Blocks all incoming traffic to every Pod in that namespace
Deletes the Pods
Only affects the Kubernetes API
quiz.explanation: An empty podSelector selects every Pod in the namespace. With Ingress listed and no rules, no incoming traffic is allowed, which is the usual "default deny" starting point.

sections.title: Auditing Your Hardening: Benchmarks and a Checklist

content.value: Hardening you cannot measure drifts away over time. Use industry benchmarks and automated scanners so that "secure" is a result you can check, not a feeling.

rows: Cluster nodes against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
Dockerfiles and Kubernetes YAML for risky settings
A Docker host against the CIS Docker Benchmark

content.value: A quick checklist before going to production

items: Image: small base, pinned version, scanned, no secrets inside.
Runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem.
All capabilities dropped; only the needed ones added.
Default-deny NetworkPolicy plus explicit allow rules.
Service account with minimal RBAC and no automatic token if unused.
Secrets come from a secrets manager, not from the image or Git.
Runtime detection (Falco) is on and alerts reach a person.

content.value: Run these checks in CI so that a risky change fails the pull request. Fixing a finding in review is cheap; finding it after an incident is not.

keyPoints: Benchmarks (CIS) and scanners turn "hardened" into something you can test.
Run the checks in CI so every change is judged, not just the first deployment.
Layers matter: image, container, pod, network, cluster, run time.

quiz.question: Which tool checks Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for insecure settings before deployment?
options: Falco
Trivy config scanning
Prometheus
Helm
quiz.explanation: `trivy config` analyses infrastructure files for misconfigurations such as running as root or missing resource limits. Falco watches behaviour at run time instead.
